extracted.intended_audience: readers, policymakers, and advocates interested in the theory and limits of free expression and individuality (general readers of political philosophy)
extracted.subtask_description: Philosophical criteria for when opinions and actions should be permitted or restricted, and for norms of public discussion and individual conduct; articulates reasons to protect free opinion, limits when speech/actions instigate harm, and the value of individuality as human development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Silenced opinion may be true
rubrics_metrics.description: If any opinion is compelled to silence, that opinion may, for aught we can certainly know, be true. To deny this is to assume our own infallibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a fundamental ground for permitting free expression: because we are fallible, suppressing opinions risks silencing truth. Do not assume the correctness of prevailing views when deciding to censor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Even erroneous opinions may contain a portion of truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Though the silenced opinion be an error, it may, and very commonly does, contain a portion of truth; and since the general or prevailing opinion on any subject is rarely or never the whole truth, it is only by the collision of adverse opinions that the remainder of the truth has any chance of being supplied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow contestation because partial truths in unpopular views can correct or complete received opinions. Suppression prevents discovery and integration of these partial truths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vigorous contest preserves the meaning and vitality of true beliefs
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if the received opinion be not only true, but the whole truth; unless it is suffered to be, and actually is, vigorously and earnestly contested, it will, by most of those who receive it, be held in the manner of a prejudice, with little comprehension or feeling of its rational grounds... the meaning of the doctrine itself will be in danger of being lost, or enfeebled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require free and earnest opposition to prevent true doctrines from ossifying into mere formal professions devoid of understanding and moral force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manner-based restrictions are impractical and dangerous to define
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who say that the free expression of all opinions should be permitted on condition that the manner be temperate, and do not pass the bounds of fair discussion—it is fit to take some notice of the impossibility of fixing where these supposed bounds are to be placed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious about regulating 'temper' or 'offence' because offended parties often claim intemperance when they cannot answer an argument. Legal or formal limits based solely on manner are unstable and risk bias toward prevailing opinions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Serious polemic misconduct (sophistry, suppression, misrepresentation) is morally grave but hard to legally punish
rubrics_metrics.description: The gravest offences in discussion are to argue sophistically, to suppress facts or arguments, to misstate the elements of the case, or misrepresent the opposite opinion. But all this is so continually done in perfect good faith... that it is rarely possible on adequate grounds conscientiously to stamp the misrepresentation as morally culpable; and still less could law presume to interfere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between intellectual malpractice (which deserves moral censure) and legal punishability (which is generally inappropriate). Encourage ethical norms and critical scrutiny rather than legal sanctions for these faults.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invective and personal abuse should be morally discouraged but not legally suppressed
rubrics_metrics.description: What is commonly meant by intemperate discussion, namely invective, sarcasm, personality, and the like, the denunciation of these weapons would deserve more sympathy if it were ever proposed to interdict them equally to both sides... It is, however, obvious that law and authority have no business with restraining either.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While vituperation is objectionable (and often harms the defenseless), regulating it by law is inappropriate; social and opinion-based censure should be the remedy, applied even-handedly where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Worst polemic offence: stigmatizing opponents as immoral
rubrics_metrics.description: The worst offence of this kind which can be committed by a polemic, is to stigmatise those who hold the contrary opinion as bad and immoral men. To calumny of this sort, those who hold any unpopular opinion are peculiarly exposed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid representing opponents as morally depraved; this weapon silences minorities and is especially damaging because unpopular groups lack institutional defence. Public discussion should instead focus on argument substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unpopular opinions obtain hearing primarily through moderation of language
rubrics_metrics.description: In general, opinions contrary to those commonly received can only obtain a hearing by studied moderation of language, and the most cautious avoidance of unnecessary offence, from which they hardly ever deviate even in a slight degree without losing ground.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Those advocating unpopular views should practice moderation and avoid provocative rhetoric to secure attention and fair consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advocacy morality: fairness, candour, and accurate representation of opponents
rubrics_metrics.description: Opinion ought, in every instance, to determine its verdict by the circumstances of the individual case; condemning every one ... in whose mode of advocacy either want of candour, or malignity, bigotry, or intolerance of feeling manifest themselves; but not inferring these vices from the side which a person takes... giving merited honour to every one... who has calmness to see and honesty to state what his opponents and their opinions really are, exaggerating nothing to their discredit, keeping nothing back which tells, or can be supposed to tell, in their favour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate advocates by the fairness of their representation and honesty, not by their position; reward calm, candid exposition that acknowledges opposing strengths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opinions lose immunity when their expression constitutes positive instigation to harm
rubrics_metrics.description: No one pretends that actions should be as free as opinions. On the contrary, even opinions lose their immunity, when the circumstances in which they are expressed are such as to constitute their expression a positive instigation to some mischievous act. An opinion that corn-dealers are starvers of the poor... ought to be unmolested when simply circulated through the press, but may justly incur punishment when delivered orally to an excited mob assembled before the house of a corn-dealer, or when handed about among the same mob in the form of a placard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restrict speech that in context is a direct incitement to imminent unlawful or harmful action; the same content may be permissible in a non-inciting context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harm principle for action: liberty limited where actions harm others
rubrics_metrics.description: Acts, of whatever kind, which, without justifiable cause, do harm to others, may be, and in the more important cases absolutely require to be, controlled by the unfavourable sentiments, and, when needful, by the active interference of mankind. The liberty of the individual must be thus far limited; he must not make himself a nuisance to other people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow individual autonomy insofar as conduct concerns only the agent; impose social or legal restraint when conduct unjustifiably harms others' interests or rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom to act: permit experiments of living so long as others are not harmed
rubrics_metrics.description: As it is useful that while mankind are imperfect there should be different opinions, so is it that there should be different experiments of living; that free scope should be given to varieties of character, short of injury to others; and that the worth of different modes of life should be proved practically, when any one thinks fit to try them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Society should tolerate diverse lifestyles and experiments in living as vehicles for personal development and social learning, constrained only by preventing harm to others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Punishment for instigating political violence requires overt act and probable connection
rubrics_metrics.description: The instigation to [tyrannicide], in a specific case, may be a proper subject of punishment, but only if an overt act has followed, and at least a probable connection can be established between the act and the instigation. Even then, it is not a foreign government, but the very government assailed, which alone, in the exercise of self-defence, can legitimately punish attacks directed against its own existence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criminalize incitement to political violence only when there is subsequent overt action plausibly linked to the instigation; restrict punitive jurisdiction to the government legitimately threatened.
